claim: During biofilm formation in B. velezensis SQR9, cells differentiate into extracellular matrix (ECM)-producers and cheater-like nonproducers.
source: During biofilm formation, cells differentiated into the extracellular matrix (ECM)-producers and cheater-like nonproducers.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy showing subpopulation expression patterns of ECM-related genes (Peps-mCherry, PtapA-mCherry) in Figure 1 and flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ECM-producers in B. velezensis SQR9 are active in the biosynthesis of genomic island-governed toxic bacillunoic acids (BAs) and self-resistance.
source: ECM-producers were also active in the biosynthesis of genomic island-governed toxic bacillunoic acids (BAs) and self-resistance
evidence: Demonstrated by co-expression of ECM reporters (Peps-mCherry, PtapA-mCherry) with BAs synthesis/immunity reporters (PbnaF-gfp, PbnaAB-gfp) in the same subpopulation as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nonproducers in B. velezensis SQR9 are sensitive to bacillunoic acids and can be partially eliminated.
source: while the nonproducers were sensitive to this antibiotic and could be partially eliminated.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy with propidium iodide staining showing cell death of nonproducers adjacent to producers in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spo0A is the co-regulator for triggering both ECM production and BAs synthesis/immunity in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: Spo0A was identified to be the co-regulator for triggering both ECM production and BAs synthesis/immunity.
evidence: Demonstrated by mutant analysis showing Δspo0A has reduced BAs production, impaired ECM production, and decreased expression of eps, tapA, bnaF, and bnaAB genes as shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Spo0A activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase to produce malonyl-CoA, which is essential for BAs biosynthesis.
source: Spo0A activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase to produce malonyl-CoA, which is essential for BAs biosynthesis, thereby stimulating BAs production and self-immunity.
evidence: Supported by data showing Spo0A positively regulates accDA expression (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and xylose-inducible accDA expression restores BAs production and immunity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4C-F).

claim: The policing system excludes ECM-nonproducing cheater-like individuals in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: the policing system not only excluded ECM-nonproducing cheater-like individuals
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry showing higher proportion of matrix-producing cooperators in wild-type compared to ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants (Figure 5A-B), and time-lapse microscopy showing selective killing of nonproducers (Figure 2).

claim: The policing system improves the production of other public goods such as protease and siderophore in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: but also improved the production of other public goods such as protease and siderophore
evidence: Supported by qualitative and quantitative assays showing wild-type SQR9 produces more proteases and siderophore compared to ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).

claim: The policing system enhances population stability and ecological fitness under stress conditions in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: consequently, enhancing the population stability and ecological fitness under stress conditions and in the rhizosphere.
evidence: Demonstrated by biofilm formation assays showing wild-type forms more robust biofilms with better stress resistance (antibiotics, salinity, acid-base, oxidation) compared to mutants lacking the policing system (Figure 5C-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2-3).

claim: The policing system enhances ecological fitness in the rhizosphere in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: consequently, enhancing the population stability and ecological fitness under stress conditions and in the rhizosphere.
evidence: Supported by root colonization assays showing wild-type SQR9 has significantly stronger root colonization compared to ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants (Figure 5F).

claim: Expression of Peps-mCherry, PtapA-mCherry, PbnaF-gfp, and PbnaAB-gfp occurs in a subpopulation of cells during biofilm formation in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: Photographs show that expression of the Peps-mCherry, PtapA-mCherry, PbnaF-gfp, and PbnaAB-gfp were all observed in a subpopulation cells of the whole community (Figure 1)
evidence: Directly observed in confocal microscopy images in Figure 1 showing heterogeneous fluorescence patterns.

claim: ECM and BAs production is generally raised in the same subpopulation in B. velezensis SQR9 biofilms.
source: the overlay of the double fluorescent reporters indicates that ECM and BAs production is generally raised in the same subpopulation (Figure 1; the yellow cells represent co-expression of mCherry and gfp)
evidence: Demonstrated by overlay images in Figure 1 showing yellow cells (co-expression of mCherry and gfp) and confirmed by flow cytometry showing positive correlation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Self-immunity gene bnaAB is specifically activated by endogenous BAs in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: since the self-immunity gene bnaAB was reported to be specifically activated by endogenous BAs (Huang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Huang et al., 2021).

claim: Self-immunity gene bnaAB is preferentially expressed in the same subpopulation with ECM-producers in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: it was also preferentially expressed in the same subpopulation with ECM-producers (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by co-localization of PbnaAB-gfp with Peps-mCherry and PtapA-mCherry in Figure 1 and flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells that don't produce public ECM or toxic BAs are killed by adjacent producers during biofilm development in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: It was observed that a portion of the cells that didn't produce public ECM or toxic BAs, or silenced in expression of the self-immunity gene bnaAB (cells without GFP signal), were killed by adjacent corresponding producers during the biofilm development process (Figure 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy with propidium iodide staining showing cell death dynamics in Figure 2 and Figure 2—videos 1–4.

claim: Producers of ECM and BAs remain alive throughout biofilm incubation in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: while these producers remained alive throughout the incubation (Figure 2—videos 1–4)
evidence: Shown in time-lapse videos (Figure 2—videos 1–4) tracking cell viability over time.

claim: The number of dead cells adjacent to producers is significantly higher than that close to non-producers in B. velezensis SQR9 biofilms.
source: importantly, the number of dead cells adjacent to the producers was significantly higher than that closed to the non-producers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing statistical analysis of dead cell distribution.

claim: Cell lysis in B. velezensis SQR9 biofilms can be attributed to BAs produced by gfp-activated cells.
source: This lysis can be attributed to the BAs produced by the gfp-activated cells, as cannibalism of B. velezensis SQR9 was largely dependent on the production of this secondary metabolism (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Huang et al., 2021) demonstrating BAs-dependent cannibalism.

claim: Only Δspo0A among mutants altered in ECM production shows significantly reduced BAs production in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: only Δspo0A but no other mutants (all with the equal cell density of the wild-type), revealed a significantly reduced inhibition zone towards FZB42, and the complementary strain generally restored the antagonistic ability (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Oxford cup assays showing inhibition zones in Figure 3A-B, comparing ΔdegU, ΔcomPA, ΔabrB, ΔsinI, ΔsinR, and Δspo0A mutants.

claim: Spo0A is a master regulator that governs multiple physiological behaviors in B. subtilis and closely-related species.
source: Spo0A is a well-investigated master regulator that governs multiple physiological behaviors in B. subtilis and closely-related species Hamon and Lazazzera, 2001; Molle et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2019b
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hamon and Lazazzera, 2001; Molle et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2019b).

claim: EPS production and biofilm formation are seriously impaired in Δspo0A mutant of B. velezensis SQR9.
source: as expected, the EPS production and biofilm formation was seriously impaired in Δspo0A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by pellicle formation and EPS production assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Δspo0A can be substantially inhibited by BAs extract of wild-type SQR9.
source: Δspo0A but neither its complementary strain nor the wild-type, can be substantially inhibited by the BAs extract of strain SQR9, while Δspo0A was not inhibited by ΔGI3 that disabled in BAs production (Figure 3C)
evidence: Demonstrated by Oxford cup assays in Figure 3C showing sensitivity of different strains to BAs extract.

claim: Spo0A participates in immunity to BAs in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: suggesting Spo0A does participate in the immunity to BAs.
evidence: Inferred from data showing Δspo0A is sensitive to BAs while wild-type and complementary strain are resistant (Figure 3C).

claim: Expression level of eps, tapA, bnaF, and bnaAB is significantly decreased in Δspo0A compared with wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 under liquid culture conditions.
source: under both liquid culture (Figure 3D) and plate colony conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), their expression level was significantly decreased in Δspo0A as compared with the wild-type, which was restored in the complementary strain Δspo0A/spo0A.
evidence: Demonstrated by gfp reporter fluorescence measurements in liquid culture (Figure 3D) and on plates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Expression level of eps, tapA, bnaF, and bnaAB is significantly decreased in Δspo0A compared with wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 under plate colony conditions.
source: under both liquid culture (Figure 3D) and plate colony conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), their expression level was significantly decreased in Δspo0A as compared with the wild-type, which was restored in the complementary strain Δspo0A/spo0A.
evidence: Demonstrated by gfp reporter fluorescence measurements in liquid culture (Figure 3D) and on plates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Spo0A regulates ECM production and BAs biosynthesis/immunity through transcriptional regulation of relevant genes in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: These results suggest that the global regulator Spo0A is the co-regulator for controlling ECM production and BAs biosynthesis/immunity in B. velezensis, which is probably dependent on the transcriptional regulation of certain relevant genes.
evidence: Inferred from gene expression data showing Spo0A-dependent changes in eps, tapA, bnaF, and bnaAB expression (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Purified protein Spo0A cannot directly bind to the promoter of bnaF in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: Results showed that the purified protein Spo0A cannot directly bind to the promoter of bnaF, suggesting it doesn't induce BAs production through direct transcriptional activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by biolayer interferometry analysis showing no binding signal between Spo0A and PbnaF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Spo0A stimulates the expression of accDA that encodes acetyl-CoA carboxylase in Bacillus.
source: Spo0A has been reported to stimulate the expression of accDA that encodes ACC (Diomandé et al., 2015; Pedrido et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Diomandé et al., 2015; Pedrido et al., 2013).

claim: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase catalyzes acetyl-CoA to generate malonyl-CoA, an essential precursor for BAs biosynthesis.
source: which catalyzes acetyl-CoA to generate malonyl-CoA, an essential precursor for BAs biosynthesis (Figure 4A; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation (Wang et al., 2019) and illustrated in the biosynthetic pathway diagram in Figure 4A.

claim: Spo0A positively regulates accDA expression in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: We firstly verified the positive regulation of Spo0A on accDA expression in B. velezensis SQR9 by gfp fusion (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 ).
evidence: Demonstrated by PaccDA-gfp reporter showing reduced fluorescence in Δspo0A compared to wild-type (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: SQR9-Pxyl-accDA loses antagonism ability towards target strain FZB42 in the absence of xylose.
source: The SQR9-Pxyl-accDA lost the antagonism ability towards target strain FZB42 in the absence of xylose, while the inhibition was significantly enhanced with the induction of xylose in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Oxford cup assays showing inhibition zones with different xylose concentrations (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Inhibition of FZB42 by SQR9-Pxyl-accDA is significantly enhanced with xylose induction in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The SQR9-Pxyl-accDA lost the antagonism ability towards target strain FZB42 in the absence of xylose, while the inhibition was significantly enhanced with the induction of xylose in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Oxford cup assays showing increasing inhibition zones with increasing xylose concentrations (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Exogenous xylose does not influence the suppression of wild-type SQR9 on FZB42.
source: Since exogenous xylose didn't influence the suppression of wild-type SQR9 on FZB42 (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: Shown by control experiments in Figure 4C-D where wild-type SQR9 shows consistent inhibition regardless of xylose concentration.

claim: accDA expression positively contributes to BAs production in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: these results suggest that accDA expression positively contributes to BAs production.
evidence: Inferred from xylose-induction experiments showing dose-dependent restoration of BAs production with accDA expression (Figure 4C-D).

claim: SQR9-Pxyl-accDA is sensitive to SQR9-produced BAs without xylose addition.
source: the SQR9-Pxyl-accDA was proved to be sensitive to SQR9-produced BAs without xylose addition, and the immunity was gradually restored with xylose supplement (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by Oxford cup assays showing inhibition zones on SQR9-Pxyl-accDA lawns without xylose (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: Immunity to BAs in SQR9-Pxyl-accDA is gradually restored with xylose supplement.
source: the SQR9-Pxyl-accDA was proved to be sensitive to SQR9-produced BAs without xylose addition, and the immunity was gradually restored with xylose supplement (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by Oxford cup assays showing decreasing inhibition zones with increasing xylose concentrations (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: Xylose-induced transcription of accDA results in enhanced expression of self-immunity gene bnaAB in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: The xylose-induced transcription of accDA, also resulted in enhanced expression of genes involved in self-immunity (bnaAB; Figure 4F, for quantitative intensity please see Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, C)
evidence: Demonstrated by colony fluorescence and liquid culture fluorescence measurements showing increased PbnaAB-gfp expression with xylose induction (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, C).

claim: Xylose-induced transcription of accDA does not result in enhanced expression of BAs synthesis gene bnaF in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: but not BAs synthesis (bnaF; Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, D)
evidence: Demonstrated by colony fluorescence and liquid culture fluorescence measurements showing no significant change in PbnaF-gfp expression with xylose induction (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, D).

claim: AccDA-derived malonyl-CoA accumulation affects BAs production in a post-transcriptional manner in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: as the AccDA-derived malonyl-CoA accumulation affects BAs production in a post-transcriptional manner.
evidence: Inferred from data showing accDA induction increases BAs production and immunity but not bnaF transcription (Figure 4C-F).

claim: Activation of accDA and bnaAB is located in the same subpopulation cells in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: The CLSM photographs and flow cytometry analysis also reveal that the activation of accDA (mCherry fusion) and bnaAB (gfp fusion) was located in the same subpopulation cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and flow cytometry showing co-localization of PaccDA-mCherry and PbnaAB-gfp (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).

claim: ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants show similar growth characteristics with wild-type B. velezensis SQR9.
source: both mutants showed similar growth characteristics with the wild-type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth curve data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of matrix-producing cooperators in wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 is significantly higher than in ΔbnaV or SQR9-P43-bnaAB communities.
source: The proportion of matrix-producing cooperators (eps & tapA active cells) in the wild-type community, as well as the average expression level of corresponding genes, were significantly higher than that in the ΔbnaV or SQR9-P43-bnaAB community (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis quantifying proportion of active cells and average FITC intensity (Figure 5A-B).

claim: The average expression level of matrix genes in wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 is significantly higher than in ΔbnaV or SQR9-P43-bnaAB communities.
source: The proportion of matrix-producing cooperators (eps & tapA active cells) in the wild-type community, as well as the average expression level of corresponding genes, were significantly higher than that in the ΔbnaV or SQR9-P43-bnaAB community (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis quantifying average FITC intensity (Figure 5A-B).

claim: Wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 establishes a more vigorous biofilm compared with ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants.
source: Consequently, the wild-type established a more vigorous biofilm as compared with the two mutants, as shown by the earlier initial progress, larger maximum biomass, and delayed dispersal process (prolonged stationary phase) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by pellicle morphology and weight dynamics measurements (Figure 5C-D).

claim: Wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 biofilm shows earlier initial progress compared to ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants.
source: as shown by the earlier initial progress, larger maximum biomass, and delayed dispersal process (prolonged stationary phase) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Shown in pellicle formation dynamics in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 biofilm shows larger maximum biomass compared to ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants.
source: as shown by the earlier initial progress, larger maximum biomass, and delayed dispersal process (prolonged stationary phase) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Shown in pellicle weight dynamics in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 biofilm shows delayed dispersal process (prolonged stationary phase) compared to ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutants.
source: as shown by the earlier initial progress, larger maximum biomass, and delayed dispersal process (prolonged stationary phase) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Shown in pellicle weight dynamics over time in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Robust biofilm formed by wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 endows stronger resistance against antibiotics compared to mutants lacking the policing system.
source: Additionally, the robust biofilm formed by the wild-type also endowed them with stronger resistance against different stresses, including antibiotics, salinity, acid-base, and oxidation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by biofilm formation assays under tetracycline and streptomycin stress (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2-3).

claim: Robust biofilm formed by wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 endows stronger resistance against salinity compared to mutants lacking the policing system.
source: Additionally, the robust biofilm formed by the wild-type also endowed them with stronger resistance against different stresses, including antibiotics, salinity, acid-base, and oxidation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by biofilm formation assays under 7% NaCl stress (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2-3).

claim: Robust biofilm formed by wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 endows stronger resistance against acid-base stress compared to mutants lacking the policing system.
source: Additionally, the robust biofilm formed by the wild-type also endowed them with stronger resistance against different stresses, including antibiotics, salinity, acid-base, and oxidation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by biofilm formation assays under pH 5 and pH 8 conditions (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2-3).

claim: Robust biofilm formed by wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 endows stronger resistance against oxidation compared to mutants lacking the policing system.
source: Additionally, the robust biofilm formed by the wild-type also endowed them with stronger resistance against different stresses, including antibiotics, salinity, acid-base, and oxidation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by biofilm formation assays under H2O2 stress (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2-3).

claim: Spo0A controls the production of proteases in Bacillus.
source: Besides the well-known regulation of biofilm matrix production, Spo0A also controls the production of other public goods such as proteases and siderophore (Fujita et al., 2005; Molle et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Fujita et al., 2005; Molle et al., 2003).

claim: Spo0A controls the production of siderophore in Bacillus.
source: Besides the well-known regulation of biofilm matrix production, Spo0A also controls the production of other public goods such as proteases and siderophore (Fujita et al., 2005; Molle et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Fujita et al., 2005; Molle et al., 2003).

claim: Spo0A is a critical switch that governs cell transition from a free-living and fast-growing status (Spo0A-OFF) to a multicellular and cooperative style (Spo0A-ON) in Bacillus.
source: it can be recognized as a critical switch that governs the cell transition from a free-living and fast-growing status (Spo0A-OFF), to a multicellular and cooperative style (Spo0A-ON) (Shank and Kolter, 2011; López et al., 2009c).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Shank and Kolter, 2011; López et al., 2009c).

claim: The punishing targets of the policing system in B. velezensis SQR9 are all Spo0A-OFF individuals, including protease-nonproducers and siderophore-nonproducers.
source: Intrinsically, the punishing targets of this policing system are supposed not limited to the cheater-like matrix-nonproducers, but all of the Spo0A-OFF individuals (cells that don't express the immune genes bnaAB, including protease-nonproducers and siderophore-nonproducers).
evidence: Inferred from the role of Spo0A in controlling multiple public goods and the co-regulation of immunity with public goods production.

claim: Extracellular proteases are accumulated more in wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 than in ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutant communities.
source: Therefore, we determined the production of extracellular proteases and siderophore among the three strains, revealing that these public goods were also accumulated more in the wild-type than in these two mutants' communities (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by qualitative and quantitative protease assays (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).

claim: Siderophore is accumulated more in wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 than in ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutant communities.
source: Therefore, we determined the production of extracellular proteases and siderophore among the three strains, revealing that these public goods were also accumulated more in the wild-type than in these two mutants' communities (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by qualitative and quantitative siderophore assays (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).

claim: Wild-type B. velezensis SQR9 demonstrates significantly stronger root colonization compared with ΔbnaV and SQR9-P43-bnaAB mutant strains.
source: Importantly, the wild-type SQR9 demonstrated significantly stronger root colonization compared with the two mutant strains losing the cheater punishing system (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by root colonization assays in hydroponic culture (Figure 5F).

claim: The Spo0A-governed co-regulation punishment system effectively optimizes the division of labor and altruistic behavior in B. velezensis population by excluding cheater-like nonproducers.
source: In summary, the Spo0A governed co-regulation punishment system effectively optimizes the division of labor and altruistic behavior in the B. velezensis population, by excluding the cheater-like nonproducers to a certain degree, consequently improving the population stability and ecological fitness under different conditions.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive data showing improved biofilm formation, public goods production, stress resistance, and root colonization in wild-type compared to mutants (Figure 5).

claim: The policing system improves population stability under different conditions in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: consequently improving the population stability and ecological fitness under different conditions.
evidence: Demonstrated by biofilm formation dynamics and stress resistance assays (Figure 5C-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2-3).

claim: Division of labor requires an efficiency benefit and alignment of interests covering different specialized individuals.
source: it would be favored if the benefit of quickly responding to drop-in nutrients outweighed the cost of having cheater-like nonproducers that reduced the ability to form a biofilm (Hamilton, 1964; Smits et al., 2006; López et al., 2009c; Joan et al., 2011; West and Cooper, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies (Hamilton, 1964; Smits et al., 2006; López et al., 2009c; Joan et al., 2011; West and Cooper, 2016).

claim: The genomic island responsible for BAs synthesis in B. velezensis SQR9 was acquired through horizontal gene transfer.
source: Interestingly, the genomic island responsible for BAs synthesis in B. velezensis SQR9 acquired through HGT, not only acts as a weapon for antagonizing closely related competitors (Wang et al., 2019), but also establishes a policing system for punishing cheater-like individuals within the biofilm community.
evidence: Stated as fact with citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: The genomic island for BAs synthesis acts as a weapon for antagonizing closely related competitors in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: the genomic island responsible for BAs synthesis in B. velezensis SQR9 acquired through HGT, not only acts as a weapon for antagonizing closely related competitors (Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: The genomic island for BAs synthesis establishes a policing system for punishing cheater-like individuals within the biofilm community in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: but also establishes a policing system for punishing cheater-like individuals within the biofilm community.
evidence: Demonstrated by the comprehensive experimental data in this study showing coordinated ECM and BAs production, selective killing of nonproducers, and improved community fitness.

claim: Bacterial biofilm is a major lifestyle in the natural environment.
source: Considering that bacterial biofilm is a major lifestyle in the natural environment (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004).

claim: B. velezensis SQR9 is a beneficial rhizobacterium that forms robust and highly structured biofilms on the air-liquid interface and plant roots.
source: Bacillus velezensis SQR9 (formerly B. amyloliquefaciens SQR9) is a well-studied beneficial rhizobacterium that forms robust and highly structured biofilms on the air-liquid interface and plant roots (Qiu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2019a; Xu et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Qiu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2019a; Xu et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2011).

claim: Strain SQR9 harbors a novel genomic island 3 (GI3) consisting of four operons.
source: Strain SQR9 harbors a novel genomic island 3 (GI3) consisting of four operons, where the second, third, and fourth operons are responsible for the production of the novel branched-chain fatty acids, BAs, while the first operon encodes an ABC transporter to export toxic BAs for self-immunity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: The second, third, and fourth operons of GI3 are responsible for the production of bacillunoic acids in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: where the second, third, and fourth operons are responsible for the production of the novel branched-chain fatty acids, BAs
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: The first operon of GI3 encodes an ABC transporter to export toxic BAs for self-immunity in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: while the first operon encodes an ABC transporter to export toxic BAs for self-immunity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Production of toxic BAs occurs in the subfraction of cells with self-immunity ability induced by BAs during biofilm formation in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: Production of toxic BAs was proved to occur in the subfraction of cells with the self-immunity ability induced by BAs during biofilm formation, where the nonproducing siblings will be lysed by BAs (Huang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Huang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Nonproducing siblings are lysed by BAs during biofilm formation in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: where the nonproducing siblings will be lysed by BAs (Huang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Huang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: BA-mediated cannibalism enhanced biofilm formation of strain SQR9.
source: Based on the manifestation that the BA-mediated cannibalism enhanced the biofilm formation of strain SQR9
evidence: Stated as an observation that led to the hypothesis of the study.

claim: Cooperative interactions are prevalent among microbial communities in many contexts.
source: Cooperative interactions are not restricted to complex, higher organisms, but are also prevalent among microbial communities in many contexts (Kehe et al., 2021; Rakoff-Nahoum et al., 2016; Wenseleers and Ratnieks, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kehe et al., 2021; Rakoff-Nahoum et al., 2016; Wenseleers and Ratnieks, 2006).

claim: Cooperative systems are vulnerable to non-cooperative cheaters that exploit public goods.
source: Both natural selection and game theory predict that cooperative systems are vulnerable to non-cooperative cheaters that exploit the benefit, such as public goods including extracellular enzymes (Chen et al., 2019), siderophore (Griffin et al., 2004), or biofilm matrix (Dragoš and Kovács, 2017; Vlamakis et al., 2013) since these selfish individuals enjoy the common resources without paying their cost (Hardin, 1968; Martin et al., 2020; West et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies (Chen et al., 2019; Griffin et al., 2004; Dragoš and Kovács, 2017; Vlamakis et al., 2013; Hardin, 1968; Martin et al., 2020; West et al., 2006).

claim: Cooperation principally survives cheating during evolutionary history.
source: Intriguingly, cooperation principally survives cheating during evolutionary history (Travisano and Velicer, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Travisano and Velicer, 2004).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include kin selection/discrimination.
source: These strategies mainly include kin selection/discrimination (Özkaya et al., 2017; Diggle et al., 2007; McNally et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Özkaya et al., 2017; Diggle et al., 2007; McNally et al., 2017).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include facultative cooperation regulated by quorum-sensing systems.
source: facultative cooperation regulated by a quorum-sensing (QS) system (Allen et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Allen et al., 2016).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include nutrient fitness cost.
source: or nutrient fitness cost (Sexton and Schuster, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Sexton and Schuster, 2017).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include coupling production of public and private goods.
source: coupling production of public and private goods (Dandekar et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Dandekar et al., 2012).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include punishment of cheating individuals by cooperator-produced antibiotics.
source: punishment of cheating individuals by cooperator-produced antibiotics (García-Contreras et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (García-Contreras et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include partial privatization of public goods under certain conditions.
source: partial privatization of public goods under certain conditions (Jin et al., 2018; Otto et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jin et al., 2018; Otto et al., 2020).

claim: Mechanisms for maintaining cooperation include spatial structuring.
source: and spatial structuring (van Gestel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (van Gestel et al., 2014).

claim: B. subtilis colony differentiates into surfactin-producing and matrix-producing cells during sliding motility.
source: For instance, Bacillus subtilis colony will phenotypically differentiate into surfactin-producing and matrix-producing cells during sliding motility, where the surfactin reduces the friction between cells and their substrate, while the matrix assembles into van Gogh bundles that drive the migration (Jordi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Jordi et al., 2015).

claim: B. subtilis cells differentiate into motile cells and matrix-producing cells during biofilm formation.
source: it is known that B. subtilis cells can differentiate into motile cells and matrix-producing cells during biofilm formation (Vlamakis et al., 2008; Chai et al., 2008; Shank and Kolter, 2011; López and Kolter, 2010; López et al., 2009c; López et al., 2009a; van Gestel et al., 2015; Vlamakis et al., 2013; Kearns, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies (Vlamakis et al., 2008; Chai et al., 2008; Shank and Kolter, 2011; López and Kolter, 2010; López et al., 2009c; López et al., 2009a; van Gestel et al., 2015; Vlamakis et al., 2013; Kearns, 2008).

claim: The advantage of division of labor is to efficiently integrate distinct cellular activities, thereby endowing a community with higher fitness than undifferentiated clones.
source: The advantage of the division of labor is to efficiently integrate distinct cellular activities, thereby endowing a community with higher fitness than undifferentiated clones (West and Cooper, 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (West and Cooper, 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).

claim: Efficient division of labor relies on elaborate coordination of cell differentiation.
source: Importantly, efficient division of labor relies on elaborate coordination of cell differentiation (Cremer et al., 2019; López et al., 2009b; Lord et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Cremer et al., 2019; López et al., 2009b; Lord et al., 2019).

claim: Nonproducing cells that enjoy public goods become cheater-like individuals in division of labor systems.
source: In relative to the subpopulation producing a certain public good (e.g. cells producing ECM during biofilm formation), the nonproducing cells that can also enjoy this common good, actually become the 'cheater-like' individuals to some extent (although they may provide other contributions to the community) (Claessen et al., 2014; Otto et al., 2020; West and Cooper, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Claessen et al., 2014; Otto et al., 2020; West and Cooper, 2016).

claim: Regulating the proportion of each cell type is important for maintaining the stability and fitness of division of labor.
source: Therefore, regulating the proportion of each cell type and alignment of interests, is important for maintaining the stability and fitness of the division of labor (West and Cooper, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (West and Cooper, 2016).

claim: Unbalanced cell differentiation reduces population productivity and can cause collapse of division of labor.
source: while an unbalanced cell differentiation will reduce the population productivity and even cause a collapse of the division of labor (Dragoš et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Dragoš et al., 2018a).

claim: The coordination policing system suppresses subpopulation in fast-growing, motility phase (Spo0A-OFF state) to promote population to stationary, resource-mining phase (Spo0A-ON state) when the environment requires.
source: The coordination policing system suppresses subpopulation that stays in a fast-growing, motility phase (Spo0A-OFF state), to promote the population to a stationary, resource-mining phase (Spo0A-ON state) when the environment required (Figure 6).
evidence: Illustrated in the working model in Figure 6 and supported by experimental data throughout the study.

claim: Spo0A-dependent toxin killing of Spo0A-OFF cells in B. subtilis enhances biofilm formation and delays sporulation progress.
source: Our finding coincides with the phenomenon that Spo0A-dependent toxin killing of Spo0A-OFF cells in B. subtilis enhances biofilm formation and delays sporulation progress, which can be attributed to both eliminating of matrix-nonproducers and releasing of available nutrients (González-Pastor et al., 2003; López et al., 2009c; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (González-Pastor et al., 2003; López et al., 2009c; Huang et al., 2021).

claim: The coordination system for optimizing division of labor is relatively temperate compared to systems for excluding obligate cheaters.
source: It should be noted that the coordination system for optimizing the division of labor is relatively temperate than those for excluding obligate cheaters (Özkaya et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015), as only a subpopulation of the cheater-like individuals were killed (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing partial killing of nonproducers (Figure 2) and citations to studies on obligate cheater exclusion (Özkaya et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: The temperate nature of the policing system represents a balance between restraining cheater-like subpopulation and retaining advantages of cell differentiation.
source: we think this scene is a balance between restraining the cheater-like subpopulation and retaining the advantages of cell differentiation (Babak, 2018; Kaern et al., 2005; López et al., 2009c).
evidence: Inferred from the partial killing observed and supported by citations to relevant studies (Babak, 2018; Kaern et al., 2005; López et al., 2009c).

claim: Spo0A simultaneously regulates ECM production and the toxin-antitoxin system in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: The molecular working model of the present policing system, being Spo0A simultaneously regulates ECM production and also the toxin-antitoxin system (Figure 6), represents typical co-regulation machinery for mediating microbial social interactions (Dandekar et al., 2012; van Gestel et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data showing Spo0A regulates both ECM genes and BAs synthesis/immunity (Figure 3, Figure 4) and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: P. aeruginosa engages the QS circuit to couple production of public and private goods for placing metabolic restraint on cheaters.
source: The opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa engages the QS circuit (LasR-LasI and RhlI-RhlR systems) to couple the production of public and private goods for placing a metabolic restraint on cheaters (Dandekar et al., 2012; Whiteley et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Dandekar et al., 2012; Whiteley et al., 2017).

claim: P. aeruginosa cooperators punish LasR-null social cheaters by producing cyanide.
source: the P. aeruginosa cooperators can also punish LasR-null social cheaters by producing cyanide, where cooperators acquire immunity from the QS system while cheaters are sensitive to this toxin (Wang et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Wang et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2019).

claim: During biofilm formation and sporulation by B. subtilis, Spo0A simultaneously induces production of matrix and cannibalism toxins (Skf and Sdp).
source: During biofilm formation and sporulation by B. subtilis, the global regulator Spo0A simultaneously induces the production of matrix and cannibalism toxins (Skf and Sdp); since genes responsible for toxin synthesis and self-immunity are simultaneously expressed, the matrix producers can be resistant to these toxins while the sensitive nonproducers will be selectively penalized (Ellermeier et al., 2006; González-Pastor et al., 2003; López et al., 2009c).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Ellermeier et al., 2006; González-Pastor et al., 2003; López et al., 2009c).

claim: In B. subtilis, matrix producers are resistant to cannibalism toxins while sensitive nonproducers are selectively penalized.
source: since genes responsible for toxin synthesis and self-immunity are simultaneously expressed, the matrix producers can be resistant to these toxins while the sensitive nonproducers will be selectively penalized (Ellermeier et al., 2006; González-Pastor et al., 2003; López et al., 2009c).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Ellermeier et al., 2006; González-Pastor et al., 2003; López et al., 2009c).

claim: The similarity between B. subtilis and B. velezensis SQR9 is that Spo0A controls synthesis of ECM and cannibalism toxin.
source: In the comparison of B. subtilis and B. velezensis SQR9, the similarity is that the global regulator Spo0A controls the synthesis of the ECM and the cannibalism toxin
evidence: Based on comparison of findings in this study with previous work on B. subtilis.

claim: The difference between B. subtilis and B. velezensis SQR9 lies in the type of cannibalism toxin and its synthesis/regulation pathway.
source: the difference lies in the type of cannibalism toxin and its synthesis/regulation pathway.
evidence: Based on comparison of findings in this study (BAs in SQR9) with previous work on B. subtilis (Skf and Sdp toxins).

claim: Toxic BAs for punishment in B. velezensis SQR9 are novel antimicrobial fatty acids that mediate cannibalism and strongly inhibit growth of closely related Bacillus strains.
source: The toxic BAs for punishment are novel antimicrobial fatty acids that firstly identified in strain SQR9, which mediate cannibalism and strongly inhibit the growth of closely related Bacillus strains
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of BAs with implicit reference to previous characterization.

claim: BAs synthesis in B. velezensis SQR9 is encoded by a horizontal gene transfer-acquired genomic island.
source: also its synthesis is encoded by a horizontal gene transfer (HGT)-acquired genomic island (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Spo0A doesn't mediate BAs production/self-immunity through direct transcriptional regulation in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: Spo0A doesn't mediate the BAs production/self-immunity in a direct transcriptional regulation way, but activates AccDA for accumulating the precursor for BAs biosynthesis (a post-transcriptional manner; Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by BLI showing no direct binding to PbnaF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and data showing Spo0A regulates accDA which produces malonyl-CoA precursor (Figure 4).

claim: Accumulated BA precursor may induce expression of BA synthetase genes in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: The accumulated BA precursor may induce the expression of BA synthetase genes
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that accDA induction increases BAs production without increasing bnaF transcription.

claim: Self-resistance to BAs in B. velezensis SQR9 is mainly induced by intracellular BAs through a two-component system.
source: additionally, the self-resistance is mainly induced by intracellular BAs through a two-component system (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Huang et al., 2021).

claim: The foreign genomic island and indigenous Spo0A regulation pathways constitute a coordination system for punishing cheater-like nonproducers in B. velezensis SQR9.
source: Therefore, the foreign genomic island and the indigenous Spo0A regulation pathways, constitute an ingenious coordination system for punishing cheater-like nonproducers and enhancing clonemate cooperation.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental data showing integration of HGT-acquired BAs synthesis with native Spo0A regulation.
